newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Randgold gets $35 mln loan for Syama mine.
newsitem.headline: Randgold gets $35 mln loan for Syama mine.

text.p: Randgold Resources, the London-listed exploration arm of Randgold and Exploration Co Ltd, said on Monday the International Finance Corp (IFC) had approved a $35 million facility for the Syama gold mine in Mali.

In addition, the IFC has agreed to take some 1.2 million Randgold Resources shares in exchange for 10 percent of its equity in Somisy, the Malian company which owns Syama, and $18 million in Somisy shareholder loans.
Following the deal, Randgold Resources will hold 75 percent of Somisy.
Randgold Resources said its Syama mine had achieved fruther productivity improvements and cost savings in the June quarter.
Cash operating costs fell eight percent in the quarter to $304 per ounce while tonnes mined increased by 13 percent to an average of 42,000 tonnes a day.
The mine chalked up case operating profits of $512,000 for the quarter turning around from its March quarter loss of $114,000.
The company said it had exercised its option to increase its stake in Somilo, the Malian owner of the Loulo project, to 50 percent from 20 percent.
Chief executive Mark Bristow said Loulo would take about two years to develop and was expected to produce 140,000 ounce of gold a year over a minimum of 10 years.
Trench results from Morila, also in Mali, indicated excellent grade continuity.

Bristow said prefeasibility studiies on the Golden Ridge project in Tanzania had indicated potential annual production of 60,000 ounces of gold and a decision had been made to proceed with a bankable feasibility study.
The chief executive said the company's total groundholdings had increased to 19,387 square kilometres with the granting of new permits in Burkina Faso, Cote d'Ivoire and Tanzania.
The company's resource base stands at 11.84 million ounces of which 7.84 million ounces are attributable.
Randgold chairman Peter Flack said the company was debt-free with cash with committed non-recource facilities totalling $90 million which would be more than enough over the next two to three years.
